source.title: Scaling Laws and Symmetry, Evidence from Neural Force Fields

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. The text identifies it as published at ICLR 2026, although the supplied venue metadata says ICLR and year 2025.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling laws in neural force fields, finding power laws and compute-optimal allocations but also showing architecture- and setup-dependent exponents and a late-training breakdown under repeated data without augmentation. This refines the scope of the scaling claims in a new domain.
record.gate_note: The study measures validation loss for neural interatomic potentials, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. Its neural-force-field results bear on V3, V4, V5 and V7, but do not test V1, V2 or V6. The paper cites language-model scaling results as motivation; those cited results are not rows. Hyperparameter values used to select settings are not rows. Relevant additional results include the symmetry-loss experiment, multi-epoch training, a diverse-molecule dataset, depth/width sweeps, and test-time group averaging.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws in parameters, data and compute, plus a compute-optimal N/D split, for neural interatomic potentials (validation energy/force loss). That is a new setting with its own results bearing on V5, on V3 and V7 (transposed to this domain) and on V4 (depth/width at fixed N). It does not test language-model cross-entropy (V1), extrapolation of loss (V2) or downstream tasks (V6). Its main argument, that architecture changes the exponent and not just the constant, refines V7 rather than overturning a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with additions. The authors conclude that NNIP losses follow power laws in N, D and compute with exponents that grow with the degree of encoded symmetry (and tensor order), so equivariance matters more at scale. Compute-optimal training should scale N and D in tandem regardless of architecture, mirroring Chinchilla. In multi-epoch training, power laws hold for tens of epochs, but unconstrained models need augmentation to avoid late breakdown. A symmetry loss or test-time averaging does not change the compute or parameter exponents, so neither substitutes for an equivariant architecture.
record.recipe_differences: This is a neural-force-field study using validation force-field loss rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. It adapts scaling-law and compute-optimal analyses to message-passing architectures and reports both FLOPs and GPU-hours.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with architecture and symmetry order, dataset composition, depth/width, repeated-data training and use of data augmentation, symmetry loss, and compute measure (FLOPs versus GPU-hours).

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling exponents rise with the degree of built-in symmetry (unconstrained < EGNN < GemNet-OC < eSEN; eSEN ℓmax 4 > ℓmax 2). Performance gaps therefore widen with scale instead of architecture changing only a constant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inductive biases such as equivariance change scaling exponents, not just multiplicative constants.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla transformers without locality or equivariance fail to learn the force-field task, with curves saturating rapidly (Fig. 16). Increasing the number of EGNN vector channels lowers loss (Fig. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some architectures do not enter a power-law regime at all on geometric tasks.

record.problems: The study is limited to academic-scale neural interatomic potentials and a specific OpenMol neutral-molecule dataset for its main experiments. Training is costly, so the authors do not tune all hyperparameters, including weight decay. eSEN uses hyperparameters adopted from prior work rather than a comparable tuning sweep. Some depth results are presented in plots without numeric values in the text. Fits assume L∞ ≈ 0 for the reported force-field scaling, and the paper notes GemNet-OC learning curves are noisy. The study does not test language-model cross-entropy or downstream task predictability.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining cross-entropy is measured; only NNIP validation energy/force loss.
No held-out prediction of larger-run losses from small-run fits. The 'extrapolate' label in Fig. 2 concerns the FLOP constant κ, not loss.
No language models, and no Kaplan-vs-Hoffmann comparison. The allocation is derived from the sum-power-law fit (approach 3), not from IsoFLOP profiles.
Only depth/width at N≈1M for three architectures (no eSEN), and no numeric loss differences. Other shape details (heads, ratios) are not tested.
No image/video, fine-tuning or transfer settings.
No downstream tasks. The paper notes direct-force pretraining may not transfer to downstream physical tasks but does not measure this.
Parameter-counting conventions and LR schedule are not varied (a schedule-free optimizer is used throughout). L∞ is fixed at ≈0 rather than compared.

missing.what: Two fitting methods (compute-optimal frontier vs sum-power-law, Table 1) give γc 0.142/0.146, 0.173/0.195, 0.255/0.256 and 0.403/0.392. This directly bears on fitting-method dependence.
eSEN ℓmax=2 gives L(C)=0.51C^-0.35, vs 0.70C^-0.40 at ℓmax=4: an exponent change within one architecture.
Under repeated data, eSEN L(C)=0.73C^-0.38 vs augmented MPNN 0.96C^-0.14, with the gap growing with compute. r30 lacks this numeric fit.

record.verdict_notes: This is a non-LM domain. V3 and V4 links are kept as transpositions of LM claims and should be read as such. L∞ is fixed at ≈0 by assumption, which affects exponent values. eSEN hyperparameters were not tuned like the other architectures. Changed r25 from reversed to partial: depth sensitivity is real but figure-only, and is not the opposite of V4's effect. Dropped the record's V7 limits_scope based on r29–r30 and folded the conditional breakdown into the r28 supports/limits pairing.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy of language models.
It fits scaling relationships and plots data points, but does not report a test in which fits from small runs predict the losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal allocation for neural force fields, not language models, and does not compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann language-model setups.
Tests depth/width effects at approximately 1M parameters in three neural force-field architectures, not language models or a broad range of architecture details.
Tests neural force fields and selected repeated-data, augmentation, and dataset settings; does not test image/video models, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance or relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance is tested.

Shows architecture, dataset, training-regime and fitting-related differences in neural force fields, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions or compare alternative fitting methods.
